passages.title: The Lost Art of Murex Purple
passages.text:
In the ancient Mediterranean, the colour purple was worth more than gold. The dye, known as Tyrian purple, was extracted from the glands of thousands of small sea snails called Murex. It took an estimated 10,000 snails to produce just one gram of the brilliant dye, making it so expensive that only emperors and high-ranking priests could wear garments coloured with it. The process was both laborious and highly malodorous, requiring the snails to be crushed and boiled for days in lead vats.

So exclusive was the colour that Roman emperors passed laws forbidding anyone outside the imperial family from wearing it, on pain of death. The dye became a symbol of power and authority across the Mediterranean. Even a single stripe of purple on a toga indicated senatorial rank. As a result, Tyrian purple was not only a luxury item but also a political tool, controlling who could display status through colour.

The knowledge of the dye’s production was slowly eroded by wars and the decline of the Roman Empire. When Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453 CE, the last workshops producing Tyrian purple were destroyed. The secret formula, passed down through generations of dyers, vanished overnight. For centuries, the brilliant purple of the ancients remained a mystery, known only from faded manuscripts and archaeological fragments.

Today, a handful of researchers in Tunisia and Lebanon are trying to resurrect the ancient craft. By studying ancient texts and analysing residues on pottery shards, they have managed to recreate small quantities of the dye. The experiments have shown that the process was even more complex than historians had imagined, requiring precise temperature control and specific timing. The rediscovery of Tyrian purple could benefit modern textile industries, offering a natural, sustainable alternative to synthetic dyes.

Moreover, the revival of Murex purple is not just about chemistry. It is a journey into the cultural and economic heart of the ancient world. The colour that once adorned the robes of Cleopatra and the curtains of the Temple of Solomon is being recreated today, reconnecting us with our past. The hope is that one day, this ancient luxury will be accessible to everyone, not just the imperial elite.

questions.q: 1. What was Tyrian purple made from?
questions.justification: The text explicitly states that the dye was extracted from the glands of small sea snails called Murex. Sea snails are the source, not minerals, berries, or chemicals.

questions.q: 2. Why was the colour purple restricted to emperors?
options: It was extremely expensive to produce
It was too bright for common people
questions.justification: The passage explains that it took 10,000 snails to produce just one gram, making it more valuable than gold. This extreme cost is why only emperors and high-ranking priests could afford it, and why laws restricted its use.

questions.q: 3. How many snails were needed to produce one gram of the dye?
questions.justification: The passage states clearly 'an estimated 10,000 snails to produce just one gram'. This highlights the incredible effort required.

questions.q: 4. What happened to the knowledge of Tyrian purple production?
options: It was recorded in the Bible
It was lost when Constantinople fell
It was sold to the Chinese
It was taken to Rome and preserved
questions.justification: The text mentions that when Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453 CE, the last workshops were destroyed and the secret formula vanished.

questions.q: 5. Why are modern researchers trying to recreate the dye?
options: To benefit modern textile industries with a natural alternative
questions.justification: The final paragraphs explain that recreating the dye could offer a natural, sustainable alternative to synthetic dyes, benefiting modern textile industries.

passages.title: The Underground City That Breathes
passages.text:
Beneath the streets of Montreal, Canada, lies a sprawling network of tunnels stretching 32 kilometres. Known as the Underground City or RÉSO, this subterranean labyrinth connects shopping centres, office buildings, hotels, and universities, enabling residents to escape the harsh Canadian winter for months at a time. The system began in the 1960s with a single tunnel linking Place Ville Marie to the Queen Elizabeth Hotel.

Over the decades it grew organically, with no overall master plan, yet today it carries over 500,000 people daily. The tunnels are lined with over 1,600 boutiques, restaurants, movie theatres, and even art installations. Commuters can travel from their apartments to their offices without ever stepping outside, a blessing when temperatures drop below -30°C.

Despite its name, the Underground City is not purely below ground; much of it consists of indoor walkways at street level and above. It features green spaces, water fountains, and natural light shafts that simulate daylight. Engineers have designed the ventilation system to mimic fresh air, making the environment surprisingly pleasant. The RÉSO has become a model for urban planners worldwide, who study how this accidental wonder keeps a cold city warm and pedestrian-friendly.

However, the Underground City also faces challenges. Its labyrinthine nature can confuse visitors, and parts of it feel dated. Maintenance is costly, and integrating new developments into the existing network requires complex negotiations between private and public stakeholders. Despite these issues, Montrealers have embraced the RÉSO as an integral part of their identity, a refuge from winter and a symbol of the city's innovative spirit.

Looking forward, there are plans to extend the network even further, connecting new universities and hospitals. The vision is to create a fully integrated urban environment where people can live, work, and play indoors during extreme weather, a concept that might become increasingly relevant as climate change brings more unpredictable weather to cities around the globe.

questions.q: 8. How many people use the network daily?

questions.q: 9. What makes the RÉSO feel natural despite being underground?
options: Green spaces, water fountains, and light shafts
questions.justification: The text mentions green spaces, water fountains, and natural light shafts that simulate daylight, making the environment pleasant.

questions.q: 10. What do urban planners from other cities do with the RÉSO?
questions.justification: The passage says 'urban planners worldwide study how this accidental wonder keeps a cold city warm and pedestrian-friendly'.
